Magenta spikes on new ash and burnt ground: the first plant back after a fall of ash.
The valleys' grass: green all year where the ground is warm, the hunters' horses and the strays both graze it.
Cairns along the trails; the Kimr's aurochs-horn markers; the Fellgangs' stone signs.
Tall reeds round the tarns' warm margins, where the springs run in.
Pumice, glassy black obsidian (the hunters knap it) and red scoria on the ash.
Yellow sulphur grown round the fumaroles' throats: the gatherers break it off.
Mineral: nothing eats it.
A cut jar bleeds rust and gives a tingle: the strand's one battery you can hold.
The ochre wader crops the frills (PLAN.md section 8).

harvest.wood: none (mineral: ochre and red oxide, a pigment)
harvest.notes: The red of an oxblood lacquer (proposed, PLAN.md section 10).

harvest.wood: none (mineral: the dead cords are sulfur, a small, clean source)
harvest.notes: Burns blue, choking.
Little upright trees of a clubmoss on the warm crust; the spores are a powder for burns.
The opaline canes ring when struck; broken ones are sharp as obsidian. Gathered whole for wind chimes and fishing floats.
Gelatinous mounds of the mats on the run-off's banks, orange and green.
A tea of the leaves for fevers; the wood burns hot and clean.
Pads on the warm water of the Stair's lower pools and the creek, yellow and pink flowers; the rhizome roasts like a potato.
Campylopus in tight cushions over the warm sinter, gold-green.
The leaves are split and woven; the orange keys of the fruit are boiled in the springs' run-off.
Yellowstone's thermal panic grass: green in the warm crust's steam all year, reddening where the ground is hottest.
Along the warm creek; cut and dried in the steam it is a quick, hot fuel.

name: Silica snag (a hypertree the sinter killed)

harvest.notes: The dead wood is turning to stone: its socks are opal. Split for whetstones.
The fan drips a mineral water: travellers drink it when they must. Never cut: the steam behind it is scalding.
Krator's own: orange filaments a metre long streaming in the warm run-off, the mats grown into weed.
Christella's kin: it fronds out on warm ground where nothing else is green.
Tufts of dry grass in the wadis' floors, where the rare runoff soaks in.
Hard red-brown tubes that flush scarlet in the heat; a red dye.
White woolly balls in the fellfield of the high walls.
A dense grey dome of fused stems, a rust heart. The goats' fodder.
A fine fur of rusty tubes: the cold desert's "grass". Fodder.
Living-pebble plates among the real stones.
A flat spiral crust that opens after the rare rain.
A low bristle of sealed sacs on wiry stems. Fodder for the ostriches.
Jointed, salt-tolerant tufts in the Deep's hollows and at the foot of the ramps: the abyssal desert's samphire, the only green on the floor.
Orange, yellow and grey-green rosettes on the walls' rock and the boulders.
Spiral-leaved begonias in the wet shade (the S highlands' habit, PLAN.md section 3); a poultice for burns.
The open benches' lush grass, grazed by the Free Giants' millipedes.
Waist-high fronds under the canopy on every bench; the young crosiers are eaten in spring.
Long green-gold tresses off the boulders and fallen columns in the wet.
The Free Giants' wet paddies on Terrace II, fed by the falls' spray: grain for Tallwalls.
The banks of the Clodosriba and the plunge basins.
Cushions half a metre deep where the falls' spray and the cloud sit; the basalt under them never dries.
Clumps of slender canes that arch over the river like a phoenix's tail. The canes are lashed into the river's rafts; the spring shoots are cut, boiled and pickled.

harvest.wood: none (left standing: a village's shade tree)
harvest.notes: A crown wider than it is tall on limbs held up by its own prop roots; strands of aerial root hang from every limb. Its small figs feed the birds. The old ones by the water are a village's meeting place.

harvest.wood: camphorwood (chests, carving: moths will not touch it)
harvest.notes: The plain's great tree, its spring flush pale green to bronze. Camphor is distilled from the chipped wood: rubbed on for aches and itch, burnt against insects.

The towers' scrub forest: small, dense, evergreen, gripping the soil pockets of every ledge and the dome. The acorns sit in cups ringed like a whorl; leached of their tannin they are ground into a jelly.
Climbing fig and Boston ivy hanging in curtains off the towers' ledges.
Holly fern and maidenhair in the shade at the towers' feet and between the blades.

harvest.edible: ['lotus seeds (fresh, dried)','lotus root (sliced, stir-fried, in soup)']
harvest.notes: Round leaves held over the pond on stalks, pink flowers, seed heads like a watering can's rose. The seeds are eaten fresh or dried; the root is the pond's harvest in winter.
Crooked pines on the towers' crests, leaning out over the cliffs with their needles in flat pads: the pine of every ink painting of this country.
Moss on the crests of the stone forest's blades and in the damp of their feet.

Dendrobium on the bare rock: jointed yellow-green canes and sprays of white and pink flowers. The canes, dried and twisted into coils, are a tonic for the stomach and the throat; gatherers climb the towers on ropes for it.
A dense dark evergreen whose tiny golden flowers in autumn scent a whole valley: Guilin is named for its forests. The flowers are dried for tea, steeped in wine and boiled into syrup for cakes.
Orchards on the plain: the largest citrus, pale yellow-green, a head across. Keeps for months; the peel is candied.

harvest.edible: ['rice (the staple: boiled, ground for rice noodles)']
harvest.notes: The plain's crop in flooded fields behind earth bunds: planted out as seedlings into water, grown green, drained before the harvest when the field turns gold. Guilin's rice noodles are made of it.
The evergreen shrubs that clothe a tower's faces wherever a crack holds soil: loropetalum, sageretia, box-leaved holly. They are why the towers are green to their feet.
Tall clumps with silver-pink plumes in autumn, on the stone forest's floor and the plain's waste corners. Cut for thatch and brooms.
The pine of the stone forest's floor: straighter than the Masson pine, its needles in threes, rooted in the soil between the blades.
The beads come off as pale grit; nothing eats them.
A cut cane whistles in the wind: the Fellgangs make pipes of them.
Poisonous; burnt, its ash is a copper green pigment.

harvest.wood: none (the hollow boles are lived in)
harvest.notes: The orange velvet pods are sawn into rounds; the chalky pulp dries into gatepod chalk that keeps a year.
The tanks hold water and frogs.
The pale bark is scraped for a fever tea; the violet racemes feed the sky rays.
The rhizome spices food and settles the stomach; the bracts hold rain water.
Too hard for an axe above the buttresses: the wind-felled limbs are the timber.

harvest.wood: light timber, dugouts, fuel (the floss: tinder and wicks)
harvest.notes: Ripe pods burst into cream floss for stuffing, and the dry floss is the jungle's tinder and lamp wick; the black seeds are pressed for oil.

harvest.wood: timber (the finest red wood), fuel (the spent capsules)
harvest.notes: The woody capsules split for winged seeds, roasted and eaten wing and all; the bark is a fever tea. The spent capsules are hard, dry and burn long: the jungle's charcoal.

A woody liana that hangs from the hero boles and bleeds a sticky resin from its cut stems. Dried on a rack, the vine burns hot and smoky even in the wet, so it is the jungle's torch and kindling; the resin dresses cuts and stings.
The iridescent gum seals hulls and dresses cuts; boiled down and cooled it is a torch resin that burns bright and smoky.
The orange keys of the hanging head are chewed, or boiled down to an orange paste; the strap leaves are woven into mats.
The young croziers are boiled; the trunk fibre is cut into pots for orchids.
Clumps of slender canes that arch over the river like a phoenix's tail. The canes are lashed into the river's rafts; the spring shoots are cut, boiled and pickled.

harvest.wood: none (left standing: a village's shade tree)
harvest.notes: A crown wider than it is tall on limbs held up by its own prop roots; strands of aerial root hang from every limb. Its small figs feed the birds. The old ones by the water are a village's meeting place.

Holly fern and maidenhair in the shade at the towers' feet and between the blades.

A flytrap of a kind: two toothed jaws a metre and more across lying open on the peat, their teeth interlocked when they shut. A leg stepped between them is held to the bone; they shut in a blink and open again in a week. Danger 0.8.
A black pool whose bed is a carpet of green bladders: a foot that stirs them is sucked down to the knee. Danger 0.3. Trap pads float on it.

Fist-sized sticky red heads on thin dark stalks standing in thousands across the open flats of a hollow: the moor. Each holds what brushes it; a person walks through and comes out bleeding and sticky. The heads are a styptic.
Waist-high crimson trumpets with a cream throat, glossy as if wet: a pitfall that takes a rat or a small dog.
Sticky pale rosettes flat on the melt pools' margins, the ice tables' flypaper for the summer's flies. Their leaves curdle milk and heal a cut.
A stone the tribes set every twenty paces along the one way through a hollow. Whistle the Hum and keep to the cairns.

Hooded green tubes twisting up to a cobra's head with translucent windows and a forked red tongue: a pitfall for frogs and lizards. A meadow of them stands where the seeps run out into a hollow; the safe path crosses it.
Yellow-green banded coils lying across the floor, warty and waxy, that lift and wind round whatever steps inside the coil. Danger 1.
A dwarf tree wind-pruned to a bonsai in the pavement's cracks: round coin leaves frosted silver-blue, a coral or amber flush at the edge. The summit's one tree.

A small pale pitcher of the ice tables that holds meltwater: it freezes at night, takes what falls through the thin ice by day, and splits in spring to drop a winter's catch. A foot goes through it to the ankle. Danger 0.2.

A sundew the size of a tree fern: a fountain of arching fronds beaded with dew that holds a frog, a bird, a child's arm, and curls over it in an hour. The first trap in Korona that holds more than an insect; its dew is the rimdew's syrup, stronger.
A red tentacled mouth lying flat on the peat, a metre across: tread on it and it closes on the leg. Danger 0.6.
A fungus-tree of the dim wet gorge: a twisted dark bole and tiers of translucent peach lace fans that glow at dusk. The dried fan is a reagent (a stimulant; a tonic in small doses).
The summit's small sun pitcher: green tubes laced white and crimson at the hood, in the sphagnum of the pavement's hollows. Insects drown in it; it is the idyllic end of the rule.

THE MAN-EATER: a pitcher two or three metres tall, waxy green mottled with blood, its lid half open, a lure flower on a stalk beside it. A person who slips on its rim goes into a throat of downward hairs and digestive fluid. Danger 1. Only where the ground is poor, wet and warm (the hell field).

A thick segmented stalk out of a rosette of leaves, and on it a flower of four big pleated orange petals round a hot-pink throat, a long tongue hanging from it. The tongue lashes at what comes near and its touch numbs a limb in a minute, the whole body in ten; the petals fold over the throat on what it holds, and the floor's other traps finish the rest. The tribes milk the tongue for a hunting poison and a surgeon's numbing. Danger 0.7.

A pitcher that lives under the ground: only its waxy lip shows at grade, and over its mouth a thin membrane it covers with dead leaves. A person who steps on it tears through onto spikes of bone-hard leaf and into the fluid below; the torn flaps hang into the pit, and the membrane grows back over the mouth in minutes. Danger 1.

THE REAGENT: a pleated fan rosette in the pavement's soil pockets, each plant one colour family (crimson, lime, teal, blue, gold, mint, cream, navy, black-red) and no two alike. The dried blades are the apothecaries' dyes and reagents; a crimson one is worth a season's climb. Grows only where the summit holds a little silt, never on the bare rock.
The Throne's snare flower, here on the warm poor floor: petals that are a noose. Danger 0.5.
Tall sealed green pods on the exposed rim that split after a storm; the tribes gather the seeds.
A giant lily pad floating on a sucking pool, its edge fringed with hairs: it folds on what lands on it. Danger 0.4.
Staghorn ferns pressed to the wet wall under every seep line: the hanging gardens' green.
Eriophorum: white heads on the cold west's wet ground.
Tight green domes, a hand to a pace across, on the cold rock and the pit rims: the native margin.
The herds' pats in the grass: the people stack them for fuel (PLAN.md section 3).
Betula nana: knee-high heath on the pit chains and the bastions' feet, torn up where the herds pass.
Stipa: silky awns combing the wind over the dry floors.
The summer's colour, cropped round the herds: sage and larkspur in violet spikes, yellow composites, saxifrage and pinks.

harvest.wood: withies (baskets, fish traps, the hide boats' frames)
harvest.notes: Salix alba and S. viminalis: many stems from one foot, arching, grey-green; on every bank. Its bark is the Kimr's fever remedy.
Juniperus communis: dark prostrate mats and low cones on the dry rock and the bastions' feet.
Plates and rosettes on the boulders, the rock and the ruin (orange, sulphur, grey); reindeer lichen in sponges on the cold ground.
Salix lanata and S. glauca: grey-felted, knee to waist high on the wet ground of the cold west.
Carex in tussocks on the wet meadows, the lakes' margins and the tarns.

harvest.wood: firewood; bark for boxes and roofing; tar from the bark
harvest.notes: Betula pendula: white stems in clumps of two to four, pendant twigs. The parkland's stands; its bark tar glues the Kimr's spear hafts.
Festuca and Agropyron: the grazing ground. Tall and rank in the wet grabens, short and cropped on the chaos floors.

harvest.wood: timber (the Kimr's roof beams and ladders); the bark for tanning
harvest.notes: Larix sibirica: an open cone of soft needles in tufts, the woods of the cold west and a scatter through the parkland. The giant elk and the mammoths strip it to their reach.
Populus laurifolia and the aspen (P. tremula): the gallery woods along the streams and the lakes' margins, tall and round-crowned, trembling. The mammoths browse it flat underneath.
Banded gneiss off the dome's walls, lichened on top.
Krator's iridescent water plants, kept in the cold pit tarns: round pads that turn every colour at a slant.
An iridescent reed in the pit tarns' shallows, Krator's native refuge in the Earth preserve.

harvest.edible: ['the melons (eaten fresh; brewed where they ferment)','the seeds (roasted)']
harvest.notes: The Labyrinth's one invented plant: a giant gourd vine trailing over the warm floors and the sun traps, its melons up to a metre across, ripening late in the dry season and fermenting where they fall. The herds and the Kimr both come for them (PLAN.md sections 4 and 5).
Artemisia: grey aromatic tufts, the steppe's smell; the herds leave it.
Boiled saponin frond-wash repels leeches and Shroud-Ants along inland border trails.
Rot-proof resinous planking for skerry surf-skiffs and laminated Spear-Queen war-bows.
Mucilaginous twin-pouch salve cools salt-spray chafing and harpoon-snail stings; sacred to Yonni Twin-Queens.
Indispensable mordant moss fixing snail hypobranchial royal Tyrian-purple and crimson dyes on linen and ramie.
Dense stone-bark timber; chalky calcium-rich fruit pulp eaten sweet or burned for shell-lime ash.
Waterproof coastal thatch fronds; glassy biogenic silica spines harvested as Yonni surgical lancets and strike-sparks.
Emergency coastal broth thickener and golden-ochre mineral indicator on granite skerries.
Plaited into heavy snail-gathering creels; calcined silica-lime ash tempers Yonni hydraulic sealime mortar.
Sterile viscoelastic pitcher mucilage sets clean waterproof wound dressings and feather-fletching glue.
Cropped holdfasts burned for potash, soda, and iodine reagent along the southern kelp frontier.
A Venus flytrap of Krator's air: rosettes of traps up to 35 cm across that shut in a third of a second on frogs, large insects and small lizards. It pinches a careless hand and lets it go.
Small, green-gold and very sour, with more vitamin C than any other fruit: dried and pounded to a powder the Wings carry against scurvy.
The heart is cut from one stem of a clump, which the clump replaces; the fronds thatch and weave. Lines the wet feet of the walls.
Every new flush scarlet, so a bench in leaf looks lit; the bark tans hides.
A fonio of poor sand: fine tufts with thread-thin seed racemes, ripe eight weeks after the rains fill the pans. Wild on the pans; sown on the sand terraces round Pinnacle Rock's foot.

A liana with squat ground pitchers to 45 cm and slim upper funnels whose rims glow faintly blue at night. Its unopened pitchers are cut for cookpots: fonio or rice packed in and steamed in the pitcher.
The bladderworts of the rain pools: yellow flowers on stalks above the water, suction bladders under it that take larvae and tadpoles.

The sundews: red rosettes and forked strap-leaved plants beaded with sticky dew. Steeped in honey or spirit the leaves make a cough and chest syrup that eases cramps; the fresh dew is dabbed on warts.
Spinifex: blue-grey spiky hummocks that die out in the middle and grow outward as rings. The resin, melted from threshed leaves, is a glue: hafting points, sealing.
A swollen grey bottle wedged in the joints, pink trumpets in the dry. The milky sap is a heart poison: on arrows, and to stun fish. Hazard: poison.
Maidenhair ferns and moss in curtains under each cap rock, where the water comes out of the parting: the hanging gardens.
A rock fig: its crown on a ledge, its pale roots laced down the wall to the ground; the figs come in clusters on the roots and the old wood, the canyons' fruit and the flyers' food.
Clumps of green and red trumpets, 0.8 to 1.8 m, each with a red nectar spoon at the rim; insects and frogs drown in them.

harvest.wood: fuel (the resinous trunk fibre: torches that burn wet)
harvest.notes: Forked black trunks shaggy with old leaf bases, a fountain of grey-green leaves at each tip, lilac flowers after rain.
Carnivorous only as a young plant, with sticky glandular leaves for a season; then a plain liana climbing the walls and the trees. The jungle's own plants turn carnivore here.
The tepui bromeliad that turned carnivore: upright yellow-green tubes of waxy leaves, 1 to 2.5 m, bright in the ultraviolet and sweet-smelling; folds shut in the dry.
One tree shelters a village. Where a prop root touches the ground it becomes a trunk.
Sap in spring; the bark for boxes, canoes and tinder; chaga on the old trunks.
Acorns leached and ground into meal: the staple of the dry side's people.
Beechmast: three-sided oily nuts in spiny husks, roasted.
Withies for baskets; the bark chewed for pain.
Standing dead wood: the best firewood on the mountain.
Rot-proof wood for canoes, roofs and poles; the inner bark makes cord and cloth.
The bark plates smell of vanilla in the sun; pitch for torches and boats; the big timber of the dry side.
Pitch from the stumps; pine-bark bread in hard winters.
Every part poisonous but the red aril: eat the cup, spit the stone. Bows from the heartwood.
The red giants of the moist draws: a fire scars them and they grow on. The bark is a hand thick and does not burn; the felled wood shatters.
The fruit stinks; the roasted nut inside is eaten in small numbers. The leaves for the memory.
Leaves for seasoning and for a steam against colds.
Lime-blossom tea for fevers; bast for rope and shoes; soft wood for carving; the bees' best tree.
Thousands of years old, mostly dead wood with one live strip of bark; never cut.
Balsam from the bark blisters.
Tapped in thaw: a sweet, faintly peppery sap.
Grows where nothing else will stand the wet; the lichen on it is a wound dressing.
Acorns leached and ground into meal; galls for ink; the bark for tanning.
The tips make a tea against scurvy; the resin a salve.
The cups hold clean water all summer; travellers drink from the low ones.
Smoking wood; the bark dyes red and black.
The gum is chewed; the wood takes no rot under water.
Sap boiled to syrup; the moss it carries is gathered for bedding.
Tonewood; the tips for syrup.
Bitter raw; after a frost, cooked to an orange-red jelly, or wine.
The twisted wood is prized for bows and handles.
Inner bark eaten in famine; tannin for hides.
The moss is gathered for bedding and caulking; it grows back in a season.
Resin from the bark blisters, for wounds.
The straight poles of every boreal lodge.
Fragrant rot-proof timber for halls; the resin burnt as incense.
The furled young funnel is cooked like a green.
The nuts are cached by the nutcrackers and dug up by bears and people alike.
Balsam from the blisters for cuts; soft white boards.
Krummholz: centuries old at knee height.
Most wild trees are bitter: the sweet strains are marked and guarded.
The Ancients' lakeside orchards gone wild: every tree a different apple.
Dried on the roofs in late summer.
The pods inflate and burst into silk; the silk stuffs pillows. The sap is poison.
The chains snap at their joints; each bead roots.
Thorny thickets on the margins, orange with berries in autumn; the oil heals burns. The catalog owes the berry (KNOWN_ISSUES.md).
The wind shakes the seed out of its pores.
Grows at its head and dies behind: a green head and a grey trail, all heading the same way.
The clock sheds its seeds downwind first.
Its awns twist with the dew and drive the seed into the ground.
A metre-long fruit that drops and rolls, shedding seed: a line of seedlings behind it.
Jointed salt succulents: a finger breaks off and roots in the crust.
The spike opens from the bottom up; bees work it all day.
Each fin is a seed on a plume; the seeds are knocked out of the shed fins and roasted.
Open in calm, shut in a gust: a gust front crosses a field as a wave of closing flowers.
A climber whose winged seeds glide down in long spirals.
Cut for hay (fodder, not wood).
Hooked burrs that ride away on animals and riders.
The wind pumps the seed out of them, and they hum: a field sings in a gale.
Roots in rust (iron is locked up in the alkaline bed) and drinks the dew the metal condenses.
The magenta flowers break straight out of the bark and the trunk.
The bulbs lift away at dusk; a crushed bulb is a cooling salve.
The ripe head snaps and rolls, rooting where it stops.
Small, hard and sweet after a frost or a long keep.
The nuts split when they ripen; the resin is a chewing gum and a varnish.
The great tree of the springs: a village gathers under it.
Sour wild fruit; the rind tans leather and dyes it yellow.
Gold in its season; it sheds cotton in drifts like snow.
Curled brown and blowing about; it unfurls green after rain.
Its yellow blades come away with seed on them and kite downwind.
Silver-grey with the salt it sweats out of its leaves; it rings the pans where nothing else will grow.
Its seeds come down as half-metre helicopters; children race them.

harvest.wood: fuel (the hardest in the steppe), charcoal
harvest.notes: Burns like coal; the caravans carry it.
The whole crown is the parachute; the bare stalks stand behind.
A tier a wet year: on the old beds its height reads how long the ground has been dry.
Roots toward water and lets the far root die: it steps a metre a decade.
The funnel spins in the wind and flings its winged seeds over its rim.
A ripe plant breaks at the root and rolls, seeding as it goes; drifts pile on the windward side of anything standing.
The husk dyes brown; the wood is the cabinetmaker's.
The plant lives underground behind translucent tips that glow with the low sun behind them.
Bitter: a tea against worms and fevers.
The velvet fruit is cracked for its dry cream pulp; the seeds are pressed for oil.
The hanging pods are sawn into rounds; the dry pulp is a sour chalk.
The pitch caulks the boats; the smoke of the needles keeps flies off.
Small figs in the leaf axils the year round, orange-red going purple; the latex is a glue.
The red resin (dragon's blood) is a dye, a varnish and a wound balm.
The fans thatch the lowland roofs.
The farm and street tree, planted for its shade and its scarlet flush.
The hardest wood of the bay: the jetties stand on it; the bark is a tannin dye.
The trumpets hold rainwater; the fringe petals are steeped for a rose-scented tea.
The bark tans the nets.
Cut for mats and boats; the white heart of a young shoot is eaten.
The orange fruit heads break into keys, chewed or cooked down to a paste.
The silica-rough stems scour pots.
The bark sheds in rainbow strips; a red gum from its cracks dresses wounds.
The sap poisons fish and arrows: never eaten.
Planted as a living fence.
The gum is chewed; the pods are fodder.
The blue arils are oily: eaten, or pressed; the leaf bases hold water for a thirsty traveller.
The trunk fibre lines hearths and grows orchids.
The upright flower candles are steeped in water until it turns sweet and gold.
The spring sap is drunk fresh.
The leaf oil is a chest rub; the shed ribbons are tinder.
The pitch is a salve.
The leaf oil is a chest rub.
The seeds are roasted and shelled; the flesh round them stinks (a catalog piece, not drawn on the stage).
A bark tea for pain.
The resin at the base glues spear heads.
The gum is dug for varnish; the round cones shed winged seeds (a catalog piece, not drawn on the stage).
Light, straight-grained boards.
The heart is eaten, which kills the stem.
The orange head under the leaf tufts: the sweet base of each key is chewed, or boiled to a paste; the leaves are woven.
The bark wraps food for the earth oven; the leaf oil is an antiseptic.
The hardest burning wood in the hills.
The spring shoots are boiled.
Scented, rot-proof boards.
The young croziers are boiled.
The pod seed is roasted and ground to flour; the gum is a sweet (a catalog piece, not drawn on the stage).
Beard lichens (Bryoria, Usnea) hanging in grey-green and black hanks from the shaded larches' branches: winter fodder and a wound dressing.

harvest.edible: ['sweetroot pieces and bistort bulbils (raided: a gift is left for the vole)']
harvest.notes: Root voles store sweetroot and bistort in their burrows, as the Inuit and Yupik raided them. The vole itself is kits/fauna's.
Rubus chamaemorus in the alas bogs: a single amber berry over two or three lobed leaves.

The Rift's frill tree, a crater standby: a tapering ribbed column, a fin on every rib on every row, a splay of long fins and a pale bud at the top. On the Throne's windward kipuka its fins are fractal fronds.

Krator's own: clusters of translucent yellow bladders on short stalks round the vents, swollen with the gas they live on; they glow faintly at night. Burst one and the stink of rotten eggs carries a hundred metres. The natives use the gas to drive vermin from their stores.
Old caps broken off by the frost, bright salmon on the snow.
Cracked stone shells lined with glowing teal crystal, on rocky ground round the cones and the hills.

A crater standby of the shoulders' cold belt (the owner's reference): a few twisted stems streaked teal and dark red, each crowned with a broad salmon cap ridged like a plate coral on top, standing among the conifers in the snow. The caps freeze through each winter and thaw again; the old ones break off and lie bright on the snow.
Edible young, bitter old. The pale wood is light and rots fast.
Black glassy fronds that drink the young lava's heat: the first life on a windward flow.

Krator's own at the treeline over the glaciers: a dark slender tree whose limbs arch out and down, hung with long translucent strands that sheathe themselves in ice each night and ring like glass in the wind; by day they drip. The natives tie the strands into wind-chimes for the dead.
Blue clusters in the dark places: skylights, gullies, hollows. They light the plume's night.

The ruff tree grown to hypertree size, on the windward kipuka (the owner's, 2026-10-06: "an interesting effect... name that tree something else and keep it"). When a flow reaches the forest its collars burst in the heat and throw their seed over the fresh lava: the ruff trees on the young flows round a kipuka are its seedlings.
Brown kelp in the isle's shallows, 3-15 m down, its fronds lying on the surface.
The fans glow by night from within; a grove of them lights a vent like a hearth.
Glows at night. Carried as a lamp by the plume's people: it lasts a few days cut.
Black leaves veined red: a shrub of the seam.
Earth's pioneer of new lava (the ohia lehua's descendant): the first tree on a young flow, red with pompom flowers.
Earth's hardiest: the first life on a fresh flow, everywhere on the mountain.
A hypertree's mangrove: stands in the warm lagoon on arching prop roots taller than a man, drops roots from its limbs, a broad flat crown of glossy leaves. The bark tans hides and stops bleeding.
A slime mould. It takes over a hollow in a night and digests what sleeps on it (NOTES.md).
The tendrils sting like nettles; the natives dry them for a fever remedy.
Squat lumpy green domes in the gullies and the skylights, a pale fringe of roots on their downhill side.
Moss, lichen and filmy ferns hung in curtains from every limb in the cloud.
Inedible. The fibrous trunk makes rope that does not rot in acid.
A palm's ringed trunk with the frill tree's fractal fins: a few short ones up the trunk, then a crown of very wide fins at the top, spread like a palm's. A Krator native of the geyser isles' shores.
Clusters of tiny glowing gold mushrooms in the velvet and the gullies.
Dark red feathers that shed the ash.

Kelp, wrack, dulse, feather weed and sea lettuce on the isle's shallow rocks and sand, from the tide line to 3 m down.
Glows orange where it is dark.
Roots in a lava tube's skylight; its hollow trunk is a chimney, and the tube's warm wet air breathes out of its top as a plume of mist that its crown lives in.
Carnivorous: they close on the insects the plume drives down. Their sap is part of the arrow poison (NOTES.md).
Hangs from the parasols' caps, its pitchers and sundews fed by the insects of the seam.
Pitchers, sticky discs and toothed traps: the plume drives the insects down to them. Part of the arrow poison (NOTES.md).
Carnivorous: the runners' discs hold what lands on the water. Part of the arrow poison (NOTES.md).
Black cups that drink the drizzle.

RANJ, THE SPICE (NOTES.md): symbiotic with a fungus that thrives only in limited and enigmatic conditions; where the fungus has got into a wound the tree bleeds a red resin that seals and regrows it. In people it closes wounds and knits bone in days; too much and the body heals too much. The Throne's vent country is its surest ground; the Spice Coast farther away is another.
Red lilies along the trails and round the stumps of the cleared forest. The bulb is poison.
The leaf gel dresses burns.
The stalks make light poles and spear shafts.
Covers the shoulder's young flows.
Grows in acid water. A source of the arrow poison (NOTES.md).
Man-high tussocks gone gold in the dry season, burnt every few years and green again in weeks.
The funnels hold rain; the plume's drizzle makes it sour.
Clusters of trumpet-capped stalks from one knotted base.

Krator's own, in the cloud: a pale slender tree whose arching limbs hang veils of fine pink filaments that comb the water out of the passing cloud and drip it to its roots. The veils glow faintly at night. Its sap stops nosebleeds (the natives say).
Crimson ground cover along the acid lake and hot pools.
Blue lumps round the hot pools, crowned with anemone tufts.
Crusts, tubes, glassy bulbs and ruffles round the vents and the hot pools: they live on the steam's chemistry, not the light.
Bundles of tall orange filaments rising from the red velvet.
Seaweed torn loose and thrown up along the high-water line.
Crusts in level bands along the beds, orange, grey-green and black: the coloured cliffs' last colour. An orchil purple (proposed): the Kingdom's trade dye.
A succulent tree with rings of upturned arms, one ring a good year, the lowest the oldest. Latex (proposed). 3-9 m.
Giant jointed canes in the lake's shallows, a whorl of strap leaves at every node, stacked like umbrellas. 2-5 m.
A low shrub that grows only along the risers' ledges, so each riser is striped with level lines of green. A yellow dye (proposed). 0.5-1.5 m.
A grey shrub of stacked flat discs, each a season's flush. Fodder. 0.5-1.2 m (station 4).
The lake tread's woodland tree: a straight grey bole with four to seven flat tiers of branches, each a level plate of small leathery leaves, sky between them. 12-20 m.
A cushion that grows in terraced mounds, a step a decade. Winter fodder. 0.2-1 m (station 4).
Floating pads that grow in overlapping steps out from the shore of the sheltered bays, the oldest highest.
Lays down lime as it grows, building rimstone dams and little pools down every wet line: the Tiers in miniature. Lime (a reagent, proposed).
Keeps each year's dead crown as a skirt and grows the next above it: a trunk ringed with collars like stacked baskets. 6-14 m.
The herds' bunchgrass: its tufts sit on the lips of the terracettes, the little soil steps that line every grazed slope. Fodder.
A felted grey sage whose flowers ring the stem in whorls, one above another, five or six to a stem: the dry slopes' summer yellow, a lilac on the canyon's benches. Medicinal (a tea); bees. 0.4-1 m.
A conifer with widely spaced level whorls and bare trunk between: the tiers' silhouette on the skyline. 10-25 m (station 2).
